newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya opposition says leaders under house arrest.
newsitem.headline: Kenya opposition says leaders under house arrest.

text.p: Kenyan security forces put four leading opposition parliamentarians under house arrest ahead of a state occasion that opposition and church leaders had threatened to disrupt, an opposition spokesman said on Sunday.

National Development Party (NDP) leader Raila Odinga, FORD-Asili chairman Kenneth Matiba, FORD-Kenya chairman Michael Kijana Wamalwa and Paul Muite, of FORD-Kenya and an activist in the unregistered Safina party, were placed under house arrest overnight, NDP secretary-general Charles Maranga and other activists told Reuters.
"The police and paramilitary units have surrounded their houses and they cannot get out. They are now under house arrest. We are condemning this action in the strongest terms possible," Maranga said.
President Daniel arap Moi was to address the state Madaraka (Self Rule) Day rally later on Sunday at central Uhuru (Freedom) Park with Tanzania President Benjamin Mkapa as guest of honour.
Scores of heavily armed police and General Service Unit (GSU) troops deployed around the park early on Sunday in an effort to prevent disruption.
An explosion started a fire in a building on Matiba's property during the night, David Kabeberi, an advisor to Matiba told Reuters.
"Last night parts of Matiba's house were set on fire. Something came from outside and exploded and burned part of the servants quarters," Kabeberi said, adding no one was injured.

Central Nairobi was brought to a standstill on Saturday when security forces fought running battles with protestors after breaking up a banned rally by opposition and church leaders demanding constitutional change before elections later this year.
According to the East African Standard newspaper one person died in the riot after being stabbed. Scores of shops and stalls were looted and dozens of cars stoned in six hours of rioting.
Opposition leaders and churchmen gave conflicting signals over what action to take over Sunday's state rally, acknowledging they had little time to co-ordinate plans.
"What we want is to call on people to stay away from Madaraka Day, but to continue to agitate through a peaceful demonstration," Maranga said.
But Timothy Njoya, a moderator of the Presbyterian Church of East Africa, said protesters should whistle at Moi's speech and then walk out.
Human rights group Amnesty International, in Kenya on a fact-finding mission ahead of elections, deplored violence by the security forces in breaking up the Saturday rally.
Moi must declare elections later this year pitting the ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) against an opposition divided on ethnic, political and personal lines.

The National Convention Assembly (NCA), a coalition of opposition and church groups, called Saturday's rally to press for constitutional reform prior to elections. The government, which in 1995 promised reform, now says change is impossible within the election timetable.
"Granting constitutional change after the election is like giving medicine to a person already dead," Njoya told Reuters.
Fair elections are impossible under a one-party system and a referendum should be held to assess the desire for constitutional change, the NCA says.
